newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians say Rabin murder their loss.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians say Rabin murder their loss.

text.p: Palestinians believe their worst fears have been realised in the year since Yitzhak Rabin's assassination.

Since the killing of the Israeli prime minister by a Jewish gunman on November 4, 1995, a hardline government has come to power and peace talks launched by Rabin and PLO leader Yasser Arafat have slowed to a snail's pace.
Despite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's vow to ease a closure clamped on the West Bank and Gaza, the territories remain sealed off.
An outburst of violence in September claimed the lives of 60 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers. The Middle East is troubled by talk of a possible Arab-Israeli war.
"Palestinians expected trouble after Rabin's assassination and they were right," said Marwan Kanafani, Arafat's spokesman and a member of the Palestinian Legislative Council.
"The tragedy is that the significance of the crime of killing Rabin was not comprehended by Israelis. Palestinians realised its meaning and were affected by it," he told Reuters.
"Now we don't have a peace process and this is what Rabin's assassin wanted," he said.
Israeli law student Yigal Amir, who was jailed for life for the assassination, hoped to stop Rabin's peace moves.
Netanyahu, a Likud party right-winger, ousted Rabin's successor, the Labour party leader Shimon Peres, in last May's elections.
For weeks Netanyahu resisted meeting Arafat. He promised to keep Israel's international commitments but opposes the basis of five years of talks -- the swap of land for peace.
Israeli-Palestinian relations have deteriorated, and peace talks were only resumed after the personal intervention of U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Clinton's special envoy left Israel last month after three weeks of trying to broker a deal on a long-delayed Israeli pullout from parts of the West Bank city of Hebron.
The PLO accuses Israel of obstructing a Hebron agreement by introducing amendments to the deal signed with Israel's previous government.

"Rabin's assassination was not an Israeli internal matter. It affected us, Israel's partners in peace, because the killing has murdered the moderate, flexible trend in Israel," said Nabil Amr, an aide to Arafat.
"It was a coup d'etat against the peaceful approach in Israel and an end to Palestinian-Israeli relations which grew with the peace process," Amr told Reuters.
The PLO leadership reacted with disbelief and despair to the assassination.
Arafat, who risked his political life by signing a peace deal with the Palestinians' longtime enemy, fretted over a possible collapse of the peace process after Rabin.

Arafat was branded a traitor by some Palestinians who considered the self-rule deal a capitulation. Any collapse of the process would jeopardise Arafat's credibility and legitimacy among his own people.
Many Palestinians on the street in the West Bank, including Arab East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip still believe Labour and Likud are two faces of the same coin.
They say Rabin's killing and the rise of a right-wing government in Israel mean no change in the already bad conditions imposed by Labour.
"These people believed that the true face of Israel, concealed by Labour, would be revealed by Likud. Their argument also proved valid," said political analyst Ghassan al-Khatib.

"For instance, issues in the PLO-Israel deal that Labour did not want to implement were also not implemented by the Likud government and the closure imposed by Labour was maintained by Likud, so things have not changed much under Likud, maybe they have become a bit worse," Khatib told Reuters.
